### 🧠 Step 2: Apply the "One-Artist, One-Technique" Rule for Portraits

We now create a **mental memory rule** that simplifies recall:

> **"When I see a portrait engraved by Ryder, I remember it was after a known artist and printed in brown ink."**

This rule:
- Anchors the information in a **consistent pattern** (one artist → one technique/style).

### ✅ Why This Works

- **"Printed in brown ink"** → a distinctive and sensory detail (color) that makes it memorable. The document explicitly states: *"His plates are usually printed in brown ink and occasionally in colours."*

This rule turns a list of facts into a **single, vivid mental image**:
> *Imagine a portrait in brown ink, with a label saying "After [Artist Name]" — that’s Ryder.*

---

→ It was **after a known artist** (e.g., Kauffman, Lawrence, Abbot).

This helps you remember **which portraits** were made by Ryder, **how they were made**, and **what to expect visually** — even without reading the full text.

# 📅 Visual Timeline: Thomas Ryder’s Major Works (1746–1810)

> *Grouped by year, with categories: Line Engravings, Stipple Engravings, Portraits, and Notable Collaborations.*

## 📌 Early Career (1760s)
**Apprenticeship & Early Recognition**  
- **1766** – Entered Society of Artists with drawings  
- **1767** – Continued participation in Society of Artists  
- **1760s** – Early training under James Basire; began apprenticeship at Royal Academy schools  

> 🔍 *Note: No major engraved works yet; foundational years in artistic training.*

---

## 🖋️ 1782 – Line Engraving  
**Technique**: Line engraving  
- **"The Politician"** (after S. Elmer)  
  - Portrait of **Benjamin Franklin**  
  - One of Ryder’s earliest significant line engravings  
  - Demonstrates mastery of portrait detail and classical line work  

> 📌 *Significance*: Marks transition from apprentice to recognized engraver; shows early influence of British portraiture.

---

## 🖼️ 1802 – Line Engraving  
**Technique**: Line engraving  
- **"Vortigern and Rowena"** (after A. Kauffman)  
  - Mythological scene; historical/legendary subject  
  - Reflects interest in classical and narrative themes  

> 📌 *Note*: Though later known for stipple, this work shows his early command of line-based composition.

---

## 🎨 1790s–1810 – Stipple Engravings (Peak Period)  
**Technique**: Stipple engraving (primary style)  
- **"The Last Supper"** (after Benjamin West)  
- **"The Murder of James I of Scotland"** (after Opie)  
- **"Prudence and Beauty"** (after A. Kauffman)  
- **Nine plates** in Boydell’s *Shakspeare* edition  
  - A major contribution to the popularization of Shakespearean themes in print  
- Plates from designs by:  
  - Bigg  
  - Bunbury  
  - Cipriani  
  - Cosway  
  - Ryley  
  - Shelley  

> ✅ *Why it matters*:  
> - Stipple engraving allows for rich tonal variation and soft gradients  
> - Ryder’s stipple works are considered **among the finest of their class**  
> - Shows technical mastery and versatility across genres (historical, mythological, literary)

---

## 🖼️ Portraiture (Various Years)  
**Technique**: Line engraving (portraits)  
- **Mrs. Damer** (after Kauffman)  
- **Henry Bunbury** (after Lawrence)  
- **Sir William Watson, M.D.** (after Abbot)  
- **Maria Linley** (after Westall)  

> 📌 *Note*: These portraits reflect Ryder’s skill in rendering human features and expression, often based on existing designs.

---

## 🏰 1800s – Collaborative Work with Royal Family  
**Technique**: Stipple engraving (full-length portrait)  
- **Whole-length portrait of Queen Charlotte**  
  - Executed by **Thomas Ryder and his son**  
  - After design by **Beechey**  
  - Prefixed to **Volume II of Boydell’s "Shakspeare"**  
  - A major royal commission, indicating high status and recognition  

> 📌 *Significance*: Highlights family collaboration and prestige in the printmaking world.

---

## 🎨 Printing Style  
- Most plates printed in **brown ink**  
- Occasionally printed in **colours** (rare, but notable)
